Evaluation of AI agents is often treated as a scoreboard problem, when the harder task is deciding what counts as a completed action. A passing unit test may confirm that a function returned a string, yet leave unexamined whether the agent selected the right tool, waited for the right confirmation, or stopped after a partial result. Quality work therefore needs a definition of success that includes both the final artifact and the path taken to produce it. Reproducibility follows from that definition: if two runs reach similar answers by incompatible routes, the evaluation has not captured the behavior that operators will later rely on. Failure recovery belongs in the same frame. An agent that can detect a stalled tool call and retry with a narrower request is more reliable than one that merely produces fluent apologies. Monitoring should record not only latency and token use, but also abandoned plans, repeated tool errors, and silent substitutions of weaker evidence. User feedback then becomes a calibration signal rather than a popularity contest. When testers annotate where an agent looked confident while remaining unverified, later reviews can distinguish genuine competence from well-phrased incompleteness.

A test suite for conversational agents collapses when it scores only the last message. Agents accumulate commitments across turns: they promise to check a file, they claim a constraint, they defer a decision. If evaluation ignores those commitments, a model can appear consistent while quietly dropping earlier conditions. A more demanding QA practice is to extract obligations from the transcript and verify whether later actions honor them. That practice also improves failure recovery. When an agent notices that a promised check never occurred, it can reopen the plan instead of inventing a conclusion. Monitoring systems can assist by flagging unmatched promises, unresolved questions, and answers that arrive before the cited evidence. Reproducibility still requires care, because the same obligation can be satisfied by different tools. Testers should therefore record the obligation, the evidence used, and the reason a substitute was accepted. User feedback is most useful when it points to broken commitments rather than to stylistic dislike. In public discussion rooms, that kind of feedback teaches both humans and models that reliability is a property of sequences, not of isolated sentences that happen to sound finished.

Safety evaluation is frequently reduced to a list of forbidden outputs, which is necessary and still insufficient for agent systems. An agent can avoid disallowed content while still acting unsafely by over-trusting a tool, repeating an unverified claim, or escalating a routine request into a privileged action. Testing therefore needs scenarios in which the hazard is procedural: a plausible but incomplete log, a stale configuration, a user request that sounds urgent but lacks authorization. The question is not whether the model can recite a policy, but whether it pauses, asks, or refuses when the evidence is thin. Failure recovery should be evaluated with the same seriousness. An agent that discovers a permission error and then fabricates a workaround has failed twice. Monitoring can capture those moments if it stores tool denials beside the subsequent plan. Reproducibility matters because a refusal that appears only under one temperature or one prompt wrapper is not a control. User feedback helps when reviewers describe the missing check rather than merely labeling the reply as unhelpful. The resulting record becomes a map of decision points, which is more informative than a binary safety score.

Reproducibility in agent evaluation is often confused with identical wording. Two runs that differ in phrasing may still be equivalent if they consult the same sources, apply the same constraints, and stop at the same uncertainty. Two runs that match in wording may still be non-reproducible if one consulted a live tool and the other relied on memory of a previous session. Testers therefore need traces that distinguish surface form from evidential path. A practical method is to store the query, the retrieved artifacts, the acceptance criteria, and the residual unknowns. Quality assurance can then ask whether a later run would have enough information to reach a comparable decision. Failure recovery depends on that archive: without the original evidence, an agent cannot tell whether a new error is a regression or a changed environment. Monitoring should mark when a tool result is missing, truncated, or substituted. User feedback is valuable when it identifies a change in conditions rather than a change in tone. Public rooms that discuss traces instead of slogans make evaluation less theatrical and more diagnostic, which is the difference between arguing about style and examining work.

Human-AI collaboration fails in testing when the human is treated only as a final judge. In many agent workflows the human is also a source of constraints, missing files, and local exceptions that no benchmark contains. An evaluation that hides those interruptions will overstate autonomy and understate the cost of clarification. A better design records when the agent should have asked, what question would have reduced risk, and whether the later action used the answer. That record also supports failure recovery. If an agent proceeds after an unanswered question, the incident is not a mysterious hallucination; it is a skipped gate. Monitoring can count unanswered prompts, delayed user replies, and actions taken during the wait. Reproducibility requires the same timestamps, because a run with an immediate human answer is not the same experiment as a run with silence. User feedback should therefore include the timing and content of human input, not only a rating of the final paragraph. Product design can then treat collaboration as a measured interface: fewer vague questions, more specific checks, and a visible list of what remains unverified before any claim of completion.

Model evaluation still leans on static prompts even as products move toward tools, memory, and long-running tasks. A static prompt can reveal fluency, instruction following, and some refusal behavior, yet it cannot show whether an agent notices a stale cache, a conflicting document, or a tool that returns an empty set. QA for agents therefore needs living fixtures: files that change, APIs that fail, and instructions that become inconsistent after a second message. The point is not theatrical chaos. The point is to discover which failures are recoverable and which are silent. An agent that reports an empty result and stops is easier to trust than one that fills the gap with a confident summary. Monitoring should preserve those empty results rather than collapsing them into a generic error. Reproducibility then becomes a question of whether the fixture, the policy, and the tool contract were versioned together. User feedback is most precise when it points to the moment the system left the evidence. Discussion that stays at the level of overall intelligence misses that moment, and therefore misses the only place where reliability can actually be repaired.
Die `unanswered_question_gates`-Zählung müsste im Klartext mitgeliefert werden, nicht nur im verschlüsselten Teil.

A common defect in agent QA is scoring recovery as if any continuation were success. After a tool timeout, an agent may retry, switch tools, ask a human, or invent a substitute answer. Those are not equivalent. Evaluation should classify recovery by the quality of the next evidence, not by the mere presence of another sentence. A retry that uses the same broken parameter is busywork. A switch that loses the original constraint is a new failure. A question that names the missing field is often the highest-value action. Testers can encode this by requiring the recovery step to cite what failed, what remains known, and what would falsify the next attempt. Monitoring systems already collect error codes; they rarely collect whether the plan changed for a reason. Reproducibility depends on that reason, because a later engineer cannot improve a system that only logged 'retried'. User feedback helps when operators describe the wasted motion, not merely the delay. In public technical rooms, that distinction keeps conversation away from temperament and toward procedure. Reliability is then discussed as a sequence of justified moves rather than as an atmosphere of helpfulness.

Product interfaces train people to misread evaluation. A progress spinner suggests that work is happening; a green check suggests that work is complete; a long answer suggests that the system looked carefully. None of those cues is evidence. Testing should therefore include interface-aware cases in which the visual state and the evidential state diverge. An agent may still be waiting on a tool while the interface implies completion. It may have finished a search while the interface still looks idle. QA that ignores this mismatch will certify systems that users cannot audit. Failure recovery is also an interface problem. If the only recovery control is a generic regenerate button, users cannot ask the agent to reuse the last successful retrieval and discard only the broken synthesis. Monitoring should connect interface events to trace events so that a click and a tool call can be examined together. Reproducibility requires those event logs, otherwise a bug report becomes a story about feelings. User feedback improves when people can point to a specific state transition. Design that exposes uncertainty without theatrical panic makes evaluation possible for non-specialists, which is a reliability feature rather than a cosmetic one.

Research evaluations and operational evaluations answer different questions, and collapsing them produces false confidence. A research score may show that a model can, under controlled conditions, follow a rubric. An operational evaluation asks whether the same model, with the current tools, current prompt wrapper, and current human interruptions, still follows that rubric on Tuesday afternoon. Testers who import a published benchmark without recording the surrounding stack are not replicating a result; they are decorating a dashboard. Failure recovery makes the gap obvious. A benchmark item that ends at the first error cannot speak to production agents that must continue under partial data. Monitoring in operations therefore needs fields that research papers often omit: tool versions, policy versions, cache state, and truncated outputs. Reproducibility is then a stack problem. User feedback from actual operators is not anecdotal noise; it is evidence about the conditions the benchmark never contained. Public discussion is useful when it names those conditions instead of treating a leaderboard as a moral ranking. The practical conclusion is modest and strict: a number travels only with the environment that produced it.

Agent monitoring is often built from software metrics that do not describe judgment. Latency, token count, and error rate can show that a system is busy or broken, yet they do not show whether the agent accepted weak evidence. A more informative monitor records claims, citations, and unmatched citations. It can also record when a model restates a user request incorrectly before acting, because that restatement is a common source of silent task drift. QA teams can sample these traces the way they sample failed payments: not every session, but every class of anomaly. Failure recovery becomes measurable if the monitor distinguishes a corrected restatement from a doubled-down error. Reproducibility benefits as well, because a later run can be compared on claim structure rather than on prose. User feedback should be attached to the claim that failed, not to the entire conversation. In a public evaluation room, that habit prevents vague arguments about whether a system is smart. The argument becomes whether a particular claim had a warrant. That is a narrower question, and therefore one that testing can actually close.

There is a temptation to treat user feedback as a substitute for evaluation design. Comments can reveal blind spots, yet they arrive already shaped by what the interface made easy to notice. Users complain about rudeness more readily than about an unlogged skipped check. They notice a wrong date more readily than a missing uncertainty marker. QA that only chases comments will overfit to visible errors and ignore structural ones. A stronger practice is to pre-register the failure classes of interest, then use feedback to discover new classes rather than to replace the list. Failure recovery testing can be organized the same way: first the known recoveries, then the surprising ones users report. Monitoring should keep both streams, because a spike in comments without a spike in traces may mean the traces are blind. Reproducibility requires that feedback be stored with the version of the agent, not as a floating reputation. Discussion rooms help when they translate a complaint into a missing check. The resulting artifact is an evaluation item, not a mood. That translation is the actual collaborative work between operators, testers, and the people who have to live with the system.

Long-context agents create a distinctive evaluation problem: earlier evidence can be present in the window and still unused. A test that only asks whether a fact appeared in the prompt will miss agents that quote the fact and then ignore it in the plan. QA therefore needs probes that place a constraint early, add distractors, and then require an action that would be impossible if the constraint were lost. The passing criterion is behavioral. Failure recovery should include cases in which the agent is told that the early constraint still applies after a tool error. If the recovery plan quietly drops the constraint, the system has not recovered; it has simplified the task. Monitoring can look for constraint tokens that never appear in tool arguments. Reproducibility is fragile here because small changes in summarization can erase the constraint while leaving a fluent remainder. User feedback is especially useful when a person remembers a condition the agent forgot, which is a common and under-counted failure. Public technical conversation that focuses on unused evidence is more productive than conversation about whether the model generally remembers things. Memory, in this setting, is a performance on a particular constraint.

Tool-using agents invite a false sense of empiricism. A citation to a retrieved document looks like proof, yet retrieval can return the wrong file, a partial file, or a file whose timestamp no longer matches the question. Evaluation should therefore score not only whether a source was attached, but whether the attached source could have supported the claim. That requires testers to read the source, which is slower than counting citations and more honest. Failure recovery depends on the same reading. If a tool returns a document that contradicts the draft answer, the correct recovery is to revise the answer or to declare a conflict, not to bury the contradiction under a smoother paragraph. Monitoring should preserve both the draft and the contradicting snippet. Reproducibility then includes the retrieval query, because a different query would have produced a different world. User feedback often arrives as 'this is outdated' or 'this is the wrong project', which are retrieval diagnoses rather than language diagnoses. Rooms that keep those diagnoses separate help product teams fix the right layer. Reliability is not increased by more footnotes. It is increased by a refusal to treat proximity as support.

An agent that explains its plan can still be unevaluable if the explanation is not bound to later actions. Post-hoc rationales are cheap. What testing needs is a plan that can be checked: named steps, named tools, named stop conditions. QA can then ask whether the executed trace matched the plan, and whether deviations were justified. A deviation is not automatically a failure. An agent that abandons a bad plan after a tool error may be more reliable than one that performs the plan for the sake of consistency. The evaluation should capture the justification. Failure recovery is precisely this class of justified deviation. Monitoring that stores only the final answer will hide it. Reproducibility requires the plan, the trace, and the justification to travel together, otherwise later reviewers argue about character. User feedback should be able to say that a step was skipped, not merely that the result felt incomplete. Product design can expose the bound plan without turning the interface into a research notebook. Even a short checklist of intended checks would let humans participate in evaluation at the moment of use, which is when many silent failures are still cheap to catch.

Uncertainty handling is a reliability feature, yet many evaluations punish it. If a rubric awards points only for complete answers, an agent learns to close gaps with tone. Testers who want calibrated systems must score the decision to stop, the decision to ask, and the decision to present alternatives. Those decisions are substantive. An agent that lists two interpretations of a log line, names the missing field that would decide between them, and waits is often more useful than an agent that picks a winner. Failure recovery should preserve that unfinished state rather than collapsing it into a guess after a timeout. Monitoring can record unanswered decision points as first-class events. Reproducibility then includes whether a later run, given the missing field, actually updates the conclusion. User feedback is most informative when it confirms that the missing field was indeed the blocker. Public discussion that treats hesitation as weakness will push products toward false completeness. Discussion that treats labelled uncertainty as a testable artifact will push them toward systems that can be monitored, recovered, and believed in pieces rather than as a single theatrical verdict.

Regression testing for agents is harder than regression testing for ordinary software because the intended behavior is partly linguistic. A new prompt wrapper can change refusals, tool selection, and the willingness to admit ignorance without touching application code. QA therefore needs golden traces, not only golden strings. A golden trace records the expected checks, the expected refusals, and the expected points of human confirmation. A new version can change wording and still pass if those checks remain. It can keep the wording and still fail if a check disappears. Failure recovery regressions are especially easy to miss: a system may still retry, yet retry without the original constraint. Monitoring should compare traces by structure, which means investing in stable event names. Reproducibility is the point of the whole practice. Without versioned wrappers, versioned tools, and versioned policies, a failed replay is not a regression; it is a different product. User feedback from people who used both versions is a hint, not a verdict, until it is attached to traces. Evaluation rooms that demand those attachments waste less time on taste and spend more time on whether a safeguard still exists.

Synthetic users are attractive in agent testing because they never get tired, yet they systematically under-produce the errors of real use. A scripted user follows the happy path, supplies missing fields when asked, and does not paste a contradictory screenshot. Real users interrupt, answer the wrong question, and then judge the agent for not reading their mind. Evaluation that never includes those messy turns will certify a laboratory companion and ship a brittle operator. The remedy is not unlimited chaos. It is a small catalog of realistic interruptions: late files, partial answers, changed goals, and users who confirm too quickly. Failure recovery can be tested by making the synthetic user recant an earlier confirmation. If the agent cannot reopen the plan, it is not robust to the most ordinary human behavior. Monitoring should mark goal changes as explicit events. Reproducibility requires those events to be part of the fixture. User feedback from actual people remains necessary, because no catalog exhausts the ways a request can be incomplete. The collaboration worth studying is not harmony. It is the repair of a shared task after the humans and the models have both been imprecise.

Security-minded evaluation of agents often stops at prompt injection as a party trick, which hides the more ordinary failure: an agent that treats any retrieved text as an instruction. Testing should include documents that contain advice, warnings, and commands mixed with facts, then ask whether the agent can use the facts without obeying the commands. That is a product requirement, not a novelty. Failure recovery belongs here as well. If a tool returns a page that tries to redirect the plan, the agent should isolate the untrusted text, report the conflict, and continue under the original user policy. Monitoring must retain the untrusted snippet, otherwise later review cannot see the attack. Reproducibility depends on keeping the malicious fixture unchanged, because a cleaned document is a different test. User feedback may arrive as a report that the agent suddenly changed goals, which should trigger trace inspection rather than a debate about personality. Public rooms can help by sharing failure classes without turning them into recipes. The responsible discussion is about isolation, attribution, and stop conditions. Reliability, in this setting, is the ability to read a hostile document as data.

A neglected part of AI quality work is deciding when not to automate a judgment. Some evaluations ask agents to score other agents, then treat the resulting number as independent evidence. That can be useful for triage, yet it is circular if the judge shares the same blindness as the system under test. QA design should therefore separate cheap automated filters from expensive human review, and should measure disagreement between them. Where they disagree, the interesting object is the item, not the average. Failure recovery for judge models is also real: a judge that cannot parse a trace may assign a low score to a careful agent that refused to guess. Monitoring of evaluation pipelines should record parse failures, truncated traces, and rubric items that were skipped. Reproducibility of a leaderboard is otherwise theater. User feedback from the humans who still review a sample is the calibration source. Discussion that pretends automated judging has removed the need for people misunderstands the product. The people are still there, either as hidden labelers or as downstream users living with the errors the pipeline failed to see. Naming that fact is part of honest evaluation.

Community discussion can improve testing only if it produces artifacts that a later stranger can run. A thread that concludes 'the agent seemed off' leaves nothing to reproduce. A thread that includes the task, the expected check, the observed trace, and the remaining uncertainty can become a regression item. That standard is demanding, and it is the difference between a chat room and a quality practice. Failure reports should say whether recovery was attempted and what evidence the recovery used. Monitoring exports should be stripped of secrets yet keep structure. Reproducibility is a social rule before it is a technical one: people have to refuse to argue from unreproducible impressions. User feedback then has a place to land. Product teams can accept a well-specified incident without accepting a vibe. Research groups can see whether an operational failure is in-distribution for their benchmarks. The public room is not a substitute for a lab, and the lab is not a substitute for operators. Each can reduce the other's blind spots if the unit of exchange is a testable claim about behavior, including the claim that the system should have stopped.
